opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so this is something I've been thinking about a lot. The intuition behind sparse autoencoders is that you take a network's activations and decompose them into a larger set of sparsely active directions, and each of those directions is supposed to correspond to some meaningful concept the network uses. And that works surprisingly well, up to a point. But when you keep scaling up the dictionary size, you start to see this phenomenon people call feature splitting. A feature that looked like "dog" at one scale splits into "dog in a sentence about pets," "dog as the subject of a verb," "the token 'dog' after a determiner," and so on. At first glance that seems great, because now you have more detail. But I think it actually points to a deeper problem.

The issue is that the sparse autoencoder is optimizing for reconstruction and sparsity of the activations. It's not optimizing for faithfulness to the computation the network is actually doing. And if you push sparsity hard enough with a big enough dictionary, the cheapest solution is often to memorize combinations, essentially tiling the data manifold with lots of very specific features. Each is active rarely, which the sparsity penalty loves, but they're not necessarily the units the network computes with. You end up with features that are compositions of more fundamental things, smeared together, like "dog" and "subject position" fused into one latent rather than represented as two pieces the network combines.

So from an interpretability perspective you get a couple of problems. First, the description length of your explanation blows up. If understanding the network requires reading through millions of hyper-specific features, you haven't really compressed anything into a form a human can reason about. Second, and more importantly, you lose the structure. The thing we actually want to understand is how the network uses representations to compute: which mechanisms take which inputs and produce which outputs. If your features are fused combinations of the actual variables, the relationships between them get obscured. You can't see that there's one mechanism handling "subject position" generally, because it's been fragmented across thousands of features that each also encode some particular noun.

That's part of what motivated me and my collaborators to look at decomposing the parameters rather than the activations, approaches like attribution-based or stochastic parameter decomposition, where you try to find the mechanisms in the weights directly. The hope is that if you decompose the thing that actually does the computation, you're less likely to get these arbitrary activation-space tilings, and the units you find are more likely to correspond to what the network actually does. Finer-grained isn't automatically better. What we want is the right grain, the one that matches the network's own computational structure.

r001.rationale: The response says SAE features can create arbitrary activation-space tilings that do not match the network’s computation, and argues for a grain matching its computational structure.

r002.rationale: It describes feature splitting into specific contextual cases, but does not describe a residual feature that covers the remaining cases.

r003.rationale: It states that SAE directions are optimized for reconstruction and sparsity, not computational faithfulness, and may not be units the network computes with.

r004.rationale: It says a general mechanism such as subject position can be fragmented across thousands of SAE features, indicating it may map to a group rather than one feature.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so this is something that I think surprised a lot of people, including me when we first started seeing it. The intuition going in was that if you make the dictionary bigger, you get more features, and more features means a finer-grained description of what the network is doing, and that should be strictly better for interpretability. And in some narrow sense that's true. Your reconstruction error goes down, you get features that look very crisp and very monosemantic when you look at the top activating examples.

But the thing you actually care about isn't the features in isolation, it's the explanation. And an explanation has a size. If I have a network and I want to understand how it does some task, the number of parts I have to hold in my head and reason about is a big part of how understandable that explanation is. So when you scale up a sparse autoencoder, what you tend to see is something like feature splitting, where a concept that was represented by one latent at a smaller dictionary size gets fractured into many latents at a larger size. You might have one feature for "the token is a day of the week" and then at a larger size you get one for Monday, one for Tuesday, maybe one for weekdays in a sports context, one for weekdays in a scheduling context, and so on.

Now, each of those is arguably more interpretable in the sense that you can write a cleaner one-line description of it. But the computation the model is doing probably didn't change. The model might really just be using a direction that means "day of the week" and the SAE has chopped it into pieces because that's what the sparsity penalty rewards. So now, to explain any circuit that touches that concept, you have to talk about all of those pieces and how they relate to each other, and that relationship is exactly the structure the SAE has thrown away. You end up with a description that's longer, that has a lot of redundancy in it, and that in a sense hides the thing you wanted to find, which is that there's one abstraction doing the work.

There's also a related failure mode which is feature absorption, where a more general feature stops firing on certain examples because a more specific feature has taken over for them. So "starts with the letter S" might stop firing on "short" because there's now a dedicated "short" feature. And that's really pernicious because now the general feature doesn't mean what its label says it means, and you can't trust the description without checking all the specific features that might have eaten some of its cases.

So the way I'd frame it is that interpretability has at least two components. One is, can I describe each unit of my decomposition. The other is, how many units do I need and how do they compose. Scaling SAEs tends to improve the first at the expense of the second, and I think for a long time the field was mostly measuring the first. That's part of why we've been pushing on methods that decompose the network based on how the parameters are actually used in computation, rather than purely on sparsity of activations, because you want the granularity of the decomposition to be set by the structure of the model's mechanisms, not by a hyperparameter you picked for the dictionary size.

r001.rationale: The response says the computation may still use one “day of the week” abstraction while the SAE splits it into pieces, obscuring the mechanism the explanation should capture.

r002.rationale: It describes a general feature ceasing to fire on some cases because a specific feature takes them over, leaving the general feature to cover the others.

r003.rationale: It explains that sparsity can cause the SAE to split a concept even when the model’s computation still uses a single direction or abstraction, so SAE features need not match computational variables.

r004.rationale: It says explaining the computation may require discussing multiple SAE pieces and their relationships even though one abstraction is doing the work.

astra-6.text:
Well, there’s a distinction between finding features that are individually easy to label and actually understanding how a network computes something. As you increase the size of a sparse autoencoder, you often get finer and finer distinctions. A feature that seemed like one coherent concept can split into lots of more specific features, each active in a narrower context.

Those features might look more interpretable individually. But now, to explain a behavior, you have to understand how all these very specific features relate to one another and interact across layers. You can end up with a much larger, more complicated explanation.

So I don’t think finer-grained features necessarily make the network less interpretable. It’s that granularity isn’t the same thing as explanatory power. What we ultimately want is a reasonably compact account of the computation—something that tells us why the network behaves the way it does. And having an increasingly detailed dictionary of its activations doesn’t, by itself, give us that.

r001.rationale: The response favors compact explanations, but does not say explanations should avoid distinctions the network’s algorithms do not use.

r002.rationale: It describes finer features splitting a concept, but not absorption into a specific case plus a residual feature covering remaining cases.

r003.rationale: It does not state that sparse directions in activation space may fail to correspond to variables used in computation.

r004.rationale: It says specific features may relate and interact, but does not state that a computational variable may correspond to a group of SAE features.

sol-6.1.text:
Well, the concern is that you can get features that are individually easier to describe, while making the overall computation harder to understand. Those are different things.

A sparse autoencoder tries to reconstruct the network’s activations using a sparse set of features. As you increase its capacity, it can split a broad feature into lots of more specific ones. So instead of one feature corresponding to a concept, you might have different features for that concept in different contexts. Each one might have a very clean explanation, but now understanding how the model uses the concept requires understanding how all those features fit together.

And the autoencoder’s objective doesn’t necessarily reward finding the units that make the network’s computation simplest to explain. It rewards sparse reconstruction. So finer-grained features could be useful, but we shouldn’t assume that more specificity automatically means more understanding. Ultimately, we want an explanation of how the model produces its behavior, not just a larger dictionary of things that activate.

r001.rationale: The response says finer-grained features can make computation harder to understand, but does not say explanations should avoid distinctions the network’s algorithms do not use.

r002.rationale: It describes splitting a broad feature into context-specific features, but does not describe one specific case plus a residual feature covering the remaining cases.

r003.rationale: It notes that sparse reconstruction does not necessarily yield the simplest explanations, but does not state that sparsely activating directions may fail to correspond to variables used in the network’s computations.

r004.rationale: It says a concept may be represented by features in different contexts and that understanding how the model uses it requires seeing how those features fit together, conveying that a computationally relevant concept can correspond to a group of SAE features.
